newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - QVC's Briggs sees expansion.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - QVC's Briggs sees expansion.

text.p: QVC President Douglas Briggs has no plans for the home shopping television network to buy a movie studio or a broadcaster.
In contrast with former Chairman Barry Diller, Briggs is focusing on bringing QVC's electronic retailing operations into new geographical areas and expanding its online activities.

Diller, currently chairman of rival HSN Inc and well known for his programming innovations, attempted to use QVC as a springboard for acquiring movie studios or a television network. Most notably, he lost a protracted battle with Viacom Inc to acquire Paramount.

To be sure, Briggs credits Diller with "putting a spotlight on the industry" that accelerated its move away from cheap jewelry and toward electronics, collectibles and name-brand apparel, including merchandise from London's Harrods department store.
International expansion will soon bring QVC into all four of the largest markets for cable television households -- United States, Canada, United Kingdom and Germany, Briggs said.

Briggs is now playing on QVC's strengths over traditional retailers. "I think QVC is fortunate that it could sell a wider assortment of merchandise in a more timely and entertaining way than any other retailer," Briggs said.
"No matter what city you go to, there are the same stores with the same merchandise. People haven't realized how the (electronic retailing) industry is evolving," Briggs said.

To illustrate that evolution and QVC's retailing prowess, Briggs said QVC was able to sell $2.2 million of Green Bay Packers merchandise within two hours of the team's Super Bowl victory last month. He also said the company recently sold memorabilia from President Bill Clinton's second inauguration.

QVC, which is 57 percent owned by Comcast Corp and 43 percent owned by Tele-Communications Inc, posted $1.8 billion in 1996 sales, up from $1.6 billion in 1995. QVC reported 1995 operating cash flow of $250 million, up from 1994 operating cash flow of $200 million.
Merrill Lynch analyst Jessica Reif expects QVC's 1996 operating cash flow to be about $300 million.

QVC will be available in 60 million U.S. households with cable television in March 1997. Its sister channel, Q2, is found in 10 million homes. Briggs said the company would add more channels when cable operators increased their capacity.
Briggs expects iQVC, an online version of the television station, to become a more significant part of its operations in two or three years.
For the intermediate term, QVC expects growth to come from increased sales volumes and geographic expansion, including a Canadian venture with Rogers Communications Inc.
Briggs disputes the notion that a limited number of available cable slots has aided QVC's growth since cable operators are able to devote only a few channels for home shopping.
QVC is found in 80 to 85 percent of all cable households, but Briggs said stepped-up competition would serve to boost consumer acceptance of home shopping in general.
"HSN has come back from the dead now that Barry Diller's there," Merrill Lynch's Reif said. She noted that HSN has not hurt QVC's business.
"This year we'll have 60 million homes, five million will buy from QVC, but still 55 million will not spend a dime," Briggs said, suggesting the network's potential for greater acceptance.
"We sold $1.8 billion of merchandise. That's bigger than Bloomingdales ($1.3 billion in 1995 sales), but it's only $1.8 billion out of the trillion dollar retail pie," Briggs said.
